desc:
You are given strings s and p where p is a subsequence of s, and an array removable of distinct indices of s.

You will delete characters of s in the order given by removable: first s[removable[0]], then s[removable[1]], and so on (the indices always refer to the original positions). Find the largest k such that after deleting the first k of these characters, p is still a subsequence of what remains of s.

For example, s = "abcbddddd", p = "abcd", removable = [3, 2, 1, 4, 5, 6] gives 1: after deleting position 3 the string abcddddd still contains abcd, but deleting position 2 as well removes the only c.
constraints: The values of removable are distinct and in [0, s.length - 1]
p is a subsequence of s; both strings consist of lowercase letters
hints: Deleting more characters can only make it harder for p to survive. What does that monotonicity allow you to do?
If you can delete the first k characters while keeping p, you can also delete any smaller number. So the feasible k values form a prefix of 0..len(removable).
Binary search on k. To test a value, mark the first k indices as deleted and run the usual two-pointer subsequence check that skips deleted positions.
editorial: If p is still a subsequence after deleting the first k listed characters, it is also a subsequence after deleting fewer of them (a smaller set of deletions leaves a superstring-in-order). So the predicate “k deletions are fine” is true for k = 0 up to some threshold and false afterwards, which is exactly the shape binary search needs.

To test a candidate k in O(n), precompute for each index of s the time at which it is deleted (its position in removable, or infinity). Then walk through s, skip every index with deletion time below k, and advance a pointer in p on equal letters. The check passes if the pointer reaches the end of p. Total O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
